hero.title: Types of Political System
hero.description: Examine the classification of political systems: Parliamentary vs. Presidential, Unitary vs. Federal, Monarchy vs. Republic, and the structural variations in global governance.

timeline.title: Evolution of Political System Classifications
timeline.description: Trace the historic milestones and scholars who defined the structural classifications of modern governments.

cards.details: First classification based on who rules (one, few, many) and the quality of rule (virtuous vs. corrupt), laying the groundwork for political science.
The Philadelphia Convention drafted the US Constitution, establishing a model of separation of powers and a stable executive independent of the legislature.
The UK saw the cabinet system consolidate under the prime ministership, establishing the principle of the executive being responsible to the legislature (fusion of powers).
The French Fifth Republic established a hybrid system, combining a directly elected President and a Prime Minister responsible to the parliament.
Scholars like K.C. Wheare classify systems like India as 'quasi-federal' due to unitary features integrated into a federal structure.

mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Use these visual memory hooks to retain critical facts about the Types of Political System for the UPSC Civil Services Examination.

items.title: Mnemonic 1: Parliamentary Features
items.decryption: Remember the key features: **R**eal and nominal executives, **C**ollective responsibility of the cabinet, **M**ajority party rule, and **D**issolution of the lower house.

items.title: Mnemonic 2: Federal System Pillars
items.phrase: "D-S-W-R (Dual government, Supremacy of constitution, Written text, Rigidity)"
items.decryption: Remember the core elements of a federation: **D**ual polity, **S**upremacy of the constitution, **W**ritten constitution, and **R**igidity of amendment procedure.

items.title: Mnemonic 3: Presidential System
items.phrase: "S-S-P (Single executive, Separation of powers, Presidential stability)"
items.decryption: Remember the three pillars of the presidential model: **S**ingle executive (head of state and government combined), strict **S**eparation of powers, and **P**residential term stability.

flashcards.title: Active Recall Flashcards
flashcards.description: Use these active recall questions to reinforce fact-dense syllabus details on the classifications of political systems.

items.question: What is the primary criteria for distinguishing between Parliamentary and Presidential systems?
items.answer: The nature of the relationship between the executive and legislative organs: fusion of powers (Parliamentary) vs. separation of powers (Presidential).

items.question: What does 'Collective Responsibility' mean in a parliamentary system?
items.answer: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the lower house of the legislature; they sink or swim together (enshrined in Article 75 of the Indian Constitution).

items.question: How do Unitary and Federal systems differ in terms of source of power?
items.answer: In a unitary system, regional bodies derive power from the central government. In a federal system, both central and state governments derive power directly from the Constitution.

items.question: What is a 'Republic' and how does it contrast with a 'Monarchy'?
items.answer: A republic has an elected head of state (direct or indirect) for a fixed term, whereas a monarchy features a hereditary head of state.

items.question: Who coined the term 'Quasi-Federal' to describe the Indian political system?
items.answer: K.C. Wheare, due to the presence of strong unitary features alongside federal structures.

traps.title: UPSC Prelims Traps to Avoid
items: Trap 1: Do not confuse federalism with administrative decentralization. In a unitary state, local bodies are subordinate agents of the center; in a federation, both center and states are equal under the Constitution.

Trap 2: A Republic is not always democratic. A political system can feature an elected head of state (a republic) but still operate under authoritarian, single-party rule without democratic liberties.

Trap 3: Do not assume that the President in a Presidential system is completely free from checks. While the executive is independent of the legislature for its tenure, the legislature holds veto over budgets and treaties (e.g., US Congress checks on President).
Trap 4: Watch out for options claiming that Britain has a written constitution or a federal structure. Britain is a classic example of a unitary state with an unwritten, flexible constitution.

deepDive.title: Syllabus Core Study Notes (Deep-Dive)
deepDive.description: Master the executive-legislative dynamics, structural divisions, and democratic/authoritarian classifications of political systems.

sections.title: 1. Executive-Legislative Dynamics: Parliamentary vs. Presidential
sections.content:
Political systems are categorized based on how the executive and legislative branches interact. This relationship defines the day-to-day operation, stability, and accountability of the government.

The Parliamentary (Cabinet) System

Characterized by the **fusion of powers** where the executive is drawn from, and responsible to, the legislature. Key features include:

  • Dual Executive: Nominal executive (President/Monarch) and Real executive (Prime Minister).
  • Accountability: Ministers are collectively responsible to the legislature (specifically the lower house).
  • Dissolution: The executive can dissolve the lower house before its term ends, prompting fresh elections.
The Presidential System

Characterized by the strict **separation of powers** (doctrine of Montesquieu) and a system of checks and balances. Key features include:

  • Single Executive: The President is both the head of state and the head of government.
  • Tenure Stability: The President has a fixed tenure and cannot be dismissed by the legislature except by impeachment.
  • Non-Responsibility: The cabinet members are personal advisors (known as 'Kitchen Cabinet') appointed by the President; they are not members of the legislature.

Executive-Legislative Relations: Fusion vs. Separation

A third model is the **Semi-Presidential system** (e.g., France, Russia, Sri Lanka), featuring a directly elected President with substantial executive powers alongside a Prime Minister and cabinet responsible to the legislature, creating a hybrid governance dynamic.

sections.title: 2. Central-State Power Distribution: Unitary vs. Federal Systems
sections.content:
Political systems are also classified based on the distribution of power between the central government and its constituent states/provinces.

The Unitary System (e.g., UK, France, Japan)

All administrative powers are vested in the central government. Regional units are created purely for administrative convenience and can be modified or abolished by the center at will. Key features include:

  • Single, supreme government.
  • Constitution may be written (France) or unwritten (UK).
  • No guaranteed separation of central-regional powers.
The Federal System (e.g., USA, Canada, India)

Powers are divided between the central government and regional governments by the Constitution itself. Both levels operate independently in their designated spheres. Key features include:

  • Written, supreme, and rigid constitution.
  • Bicameral legislature (essential to represent states in the federal parliament).
  • Independent judiciary to arbitrate disputes between center and states.

The Indian Model: Quasi-Federalism

The Indian Constitution does not use the word "Federation" anywhere; instead, Article 1 declares India as a "Union of States". Constitutional scholar K.C. Wheare described the Indian political system as "quasi-federal" (federal in structure but unitary in spirit) because of strong centralizing features (e.g., single citizenship, single integrated judiciary, emergency provisions, Appointment of State Governors by the President, and All-India Services). This ensures national integrity and unity while accommodating regional diversity.
